notes: The original. A megalodon's body — available from the first boss of every run.
Faster and turns harder than the shark. minLevel is 0 deliberately, so it can open a run.

The kraken. The one boss that does not come to you: it holds mid-range, circles, and fills the water with ink you cannot see through — see systems/kraken.js. Held to level 20 because it is the hardest arrival to READ, and a player meeting it as their first boss would have no idea what the ink was for. sizeMul is under the other two animals' on purpose — much of this body's length is arm, which carries no hitbox. ownNames is left FALSE: it takes the general pool plus the parts tagged for it.

The king crab. The one boss that walks: it holds the seabed and hauls itself off it at you, so the fight is fought in the layer the chum settles in — see CONFIG.enemies.bossCrab. sizeMul is the highest in the file and that is a fact about the BODY, not an escalation: a crab's radius describes its half-height (it doubles as how high it rests off the sand) while its silhouette is three times as wide, so the same on-screen size as a shark costs a much bigger multiplier. minLevel is 0 deliberately, so it can open a run — every archetype after the first arrives with a perk, and a floor-bound boss wants the reach one of those buys it. ownNames TRUE: a crab is not a fish and should not roll the pool's swimming words.

The mosasaur. The fifth swimming archetype and the only one that is not a shark, an orca or a squid — see enemyMosasaur in assets.js for why that silhouette was worth a slot. Fights like the shark does, on purpose: it chases, and the counterplay is its turning circle, which is the widest in the file (1.15 against the kraken's 1.7). What it has instead of a bespoke system is the only authored BITE besides the megalodon's — 62 degrees of gape over 1.68s — so its one committed attack is a thing the player watches happen rather than a number applied to them. sizeMul 1.6 makes it the longest final body in the game at 27.2 units, which is the whole claim this animal makes. Held to level 10 so it is never a run's first boss: it hits harder than the shark and reads the same way, so meeting it first would just be a harder shark.

The hammerhead. The one boss that hits you SOMEWHERE ELSE — it is the only creature in the game that declares `playerKnockback`, and being thrown a dozen units off your line — further than a full strike dash carries you — is most of what it does to you. Everything else about it is arranged to earn that: the highest turn rate of any boss (2.6, over the orca's 2.4), the smallest body (23.0 units against the mosasaur's 27.2), and the LOWEST contact damage of the swimmers (38 against the shark's 44), because the punishment is losing your position rather than your health. Its head-look is the tell — a hammerhead swings that skull to face you before it arrives, which is the one thing this rig does better than any other in the roster. Held to level 12 so it is never a run's first or second boss: being shoved is a new verb, and it costs most when the player has no movement upgrades to swim out of it with.

The trawler that shoots back. Rides the surface and shells the water — see systems/bossBoat.js. Held to level 10 so it is never a run's first boss: it is the one fight that is not about swimming at something.

The yacht. A SUBTYPE of the trawler rather than a seventh archetype: the same station-keeping, the same three ordnance patterns, the same systems/bossBoat.js — it is not told which hull it has. What is new is on the deck. This one arrives with GUESTS on it (CONFIG.enemies.bossYacht crewAsset/crewCount, driven by systems/crew.js), where the trawler sails alone, so the deck becomes worth shooting at: a guest knocked into the water is food, and the sharks and the orca pod will break off what they were doing to get to him. Held to level 10 for the same reason as the trawler, and shares its shuffle-bag weight, so a run that draws a boat gets one or the other. ownNames TRUE: a yacht is not a fish, and it is not a trawler either — it draws its own vocabulary, not the trawler's.
